categoryNotes.story: Concrete, dated examples for behavioural questions ('tell me about a time'). Deliberately separated from experience so retrieval doesn't surface 2007 anecdotes when someone asks what Chris does now. Always keep the date in the text.

chunks.title: Who Chris is
chunks.text: Chris Pollard is a Melbourne-based engineer who takes LLM agents from demo to production, with a decade of project and product delivery behind it. He builds production LLM systems himself, with a solo-built multi-agent platform as his flagship, and can own delivery end to end: roadmap and stakeholders through to shipped, working software.

chunks.title: What makes Chris's profile rare
chunks.text: What's rare is the pairing. Most AI hires are strong on the build or strong on delivery; Chris does both — writing the agents and the retrieval, and landing the project with the people around it. He keeps a human at the edge of every automated decision, and cares that what ships is trustworthy and actually used. He is based in Melbourne, Australia.

chunks.title: Writing about the work
chunks.text: Chris posts weekly on LinkedIn about building agents and workflows, drawing on what he has learned running business-mono. His portfolio site is itself a demo: a live retrieval agent that answers questions about his work from a cited corpus.

chunks.title: Bitcoin Treasury Solutions — Co-founder & Principal Engineer
chunks.text: Bitcoin Treasury Solutions — Co-founder and Principal Engineer (March 2025 to present, Melbourne). The company delivers structured bitcoin training for professionals, SMEs and individuals. Chris set up Avuncular Group Pty Ltd, the company behind it, runs its strategy and administration, and brought Carolyn Crawford on as co-founder; she leads the commercial and training side. Chris owns the technology end to end, including business-mono, the agent platform behind the business. The business is pre-revenue, so he is used to thinking through business problems and the trade-offs in what to build.

chunks.title: Juvare — Technical Implementation Analyst
chunks.text: Juvare — Technical Implementation Analyst, frontend and solutions delivery (December 2023 to May 2026, Melbourne). The title understated the shape of it: roughly 70% front-end web development, 20% business analysis and 10% direct client work. The product is WebEOC, Juvare's emergency and incident management platform; the company is US-owned with core server-side development based in Lithuania, so the Australian team operated as the client-facing end of a distributed product organisation. Chris mentored newer developers both locally and remotely, helped supervise onboarding, and led the implementation of a code-review system.

chunks.title: Beyond Essential Systems — Software Engineer
chunks.text: Beyond Essential Systems — Software Engineer (September 2021 to December 2023, Melbourne). Full-stack development across server- and client-side packages in a monorepo, including microservices and a React Native app. Contributed to Tupaia, an open-source health-data aggregation and visualisation platform for low-resource settings, and Tamanu, an electronic medical record system for the Pacific region.

chunks.title: General Assembly — Software Engineering Immersive
chunks.text: General Assembly — Software Engineering Immersive (February 2021 to August 2021, Melbourne). A full-time twelve-week immersive, taken across two intakes, covering JavaScript, Node.js (Express), React, REST APIs, Ruby/Sinatra, PostgreSQL and Git — Chris's deliberate, structured transition from product management into software engineering. He went straight into full-stack engineering at Beyond Essential Systems on completing it.

chunks.title: VTAC — Project Manager (product)
chunks.text: Victorian Tertiary Admissions Centre — Project Manager (November 2014 to March 2020, Melbourne). Owned delivery of the FlexiDirect SaaS platform — the direct application portal used by education providers — as product manager, from client discovery and pricing model to roadmap and release, coordinating developers, testers and UX designers to ship against strategic goals. The clearest early example of Chris leading technical delivery end to end.

chunks.title: RMIT University — Project Manager (pandemic response)
chunks.text: RMIT University — Project Manager (March 2020 to December 2020, Melbourne). Project management for RMIT's pandemic response, where the constraint was rarely technical: it was getting senior stakeholders with different operational realities to agree on a single course of action, quickly, while government direction kept changing underneath. Chris facilitated consensus across executives with competing priorities and no precedent to work from, and translated operational detail into terms executives could decide on — then translated those decisions back into something operationally workable.

chunks.title: Making operational reality legible to executives
chunks.text: The capability Chris has been paid for most consistently is being the person in the room who makes operational truth legible to the people deciding, and the decision legible to the people executing. Three separate instances: VTAC, where the clients were also the owners and priorities genuinely competed; RMIT in 2020, driving executive consensus on pandemic response with no precedent and requirements changing weekly; and Juvare, turning a government agency's business process into a built system. Three instances across a decade is a pattern rather than an anecdote — and it is the half of the profile most AI engineers cannot evidence.

chunks.title: Earlier career (2007–2014)
chunks.text: Before VTAC, Chris ran a small video production business (2007–2008), travelled, then studied teaching at La Trobe. Rather than teach, he moved into university student administration and services, working at Swinburne, the University of Melbourne and Monash, then took a project role at La Trobe that led to VTAC in 2014. It's where the delivery-and-stakeholder half of his skill set started.

chunks.title: Education and certifications
chunks.text: Bachelor of Performing Arts, Monash University (2004–2007); Graduate Diploma in Education, La Trobe University (2009–2010); Software Engineering Immersive, General Assembly (2021). Certifications include PRINCE2 Practitioner (earned in 2016 while at VTAC, now lapsed), WebEOC Bootcamp, a Bitcoin Protocol Development seminar series, and freelance website development.

chunks.title: business-mono — overview
chunks.text: business-mono is a production operations platform Chris built single-handedly as the system behind Bitcoin Treasury Solutions, where he is co-founder and principal engineer. It monitors news and podcast sources, analyses and stores what is useful in a searchable knowledge base, and runs the curation workflows built on top of it, including a daily news email. A Mastra server runs the agents and workflows, all sharing one Supabase database; a Next.js 15 app handles dashboards and human approvals. It began as a hub-and-spoke design around a coordinator agent (Simon), but most of it now runs as structured workflows.

chunks.title: From a coordinator to structured workflows
chunks.text: business-mono was designed hub-and-spoke rather than as a flat swarm: a single coordinator (Simon) routes each request to the right specialist agent — recorder, archivist, project manager, business analyst, content creator, researcher, relationship manager, marketer and compliance — behind a consistent audit trail. In practice the coordinator now does far less than Chris planned. Most of the platform runs as structured workflows, because for most jobs a workflow proved more reliable and easier to reason about than an agent deciding what to do next.

chunks.title: Hybrid retrieval
chunks.text: The knowledge base uses hybrid search rather than a single vector lookup: pgvector (HNSW) similarity, graph traversal across knowledge connections, and Postgres full-text search, so each query uses the method that fits it. Embeddings are generated with OpenAI text-embedding-3-small at 1536 dimensions.

chunks.title: Suspend / resume elicitation
chunks.text: The requirements workflow runs multi-round clarification loops using Mastra's suspend and resume: it pauses mid-workflow to ask a human for input, then resumes with that answer folded in. This is structured elicitation with state carried across turns, not a single hopeful prompt.

chunks.title: Approval graduation model
chunks.text: Operations earn autonomy in stages: an action moves from human-confirmed, to batch-approved, to autonomous as it proves reliable. High-risk actions — outbound emails, published content and CRM writes — stay human-approved regardless of track record. Trust is graduated, not granted.

chunks.title: Compliance gate in the loop
chunks.text: A dedicated compliance agent reviews advice-framed drafts against Australian financial-services (AFSL) rules, records its verdict and never auto-approves. If the copy changes, the review re-runs — governance is wired into the workflow rather than left to a final human glance.

chunks.title: Ingestion: news and podcast monitoring
chunks.text: The platform monitors news and podcast sources, analyses what comes in, and stores what is useful in the same knowledge base the agents and workflows retrieve from. That material feeds the curation workflows, including a daily news email that summarises the relevant stories with headline links.

chunks.title: Deployment and structure
chunks.text: The codebase is a Turborepo monorepo. Agents and workflows run on Railway; the Next.js web app deploys to Vercel; Supabase provides Postgres and pgvector. Vitest suites for both apps are gated in CI alongside typecheck; a separate LLM eval suite for agent routing and prompts runs on demand rather than in CI, because non-deterministic model calls do not belong in a PR gate.

chunks.title: Core stack
chunks.text: Chris works primarily in TypeScript and Node.js. On the web he uses Next.js 15 (App Router), React and React Native; for agents and workflows, Mastra; and Supabase with pgvector for data and retrieval, organised in a Turborepo monorepo. His full-stack background spans microservices and client apps. He writes end-to-end and integration tests as part of the work, not after it.

chunks.title: LLM engineering skills
chunks.text: On the LLM side he builds agent orchestration, retrieval-augmented generation, hybrid search, tool use and human-in-the-loop control flow, and treats evals as first-class — a dedicated routing and prompt eval suite, run on demand against real models, with the deterministic test suites gated in CI. His production agent work is built on Mastra; he has also prototyped pipelines with Flowise and LangChain.

chunks.title: Which models he uses
chunks.text: business-mono is model-agnostic. Its steps run on models from several providers, from Claude and DeepSeek to Google's Gemini image model (Nano Banana), so each job can use the model that suits it rather than one default. Chris builds mostly with Claude, and at Juvare he also worked with OpenAI and Copilot as development tools. The agent on his portfolio site runs on Claude Haiku, with OpenAI text-embedding-3-small for retrieval.

chunks.title: Scale and ownership
chunks.text: business-mono is a genuinely solo build: the coordinator, the specialist agents, the workflows, the ingestion pipelines and the web app were all architected and shipped by one person, across a Turborepo monorepo with CI-gated test suites. It has been under sustained development rather than built in a burst, and it runs every day, though most of its output is used inside the business rather than sent to customers. The repository is public, so the scope can be inspected rather than taken on trust.

chunks.title: How Chris works
chunks.text: Chris works docs-first — per-agent specifications, a design brief and a defined brand voice sit alongside the code — and brings design thinking to systems, not just interfaces. Deterministic tests and typecheck gate every change in CI, and a separate eval suite exercises agent routing and prompts against real models on demand, so behaviour is verified rather than assumed.

chunks.title: How Chris changes a live workflow
chunks.text: Chris changes business-mono incrementally. He user-tests before changing or adding pieces of a workflow, adds them one at a time, and reads the real output every day. Anything that leaves the business still goes through human approval, so new pieces earn trust before they matter.

chunks.title: How much experience does he have?
chunks.text: Chris pairs a decade of project and product delivery with hands-on engineering. He moved into software in 2021 — full-stack roles at Beyond Essential Systems and Juvare — and now builds multi-agent LLM systems, so he can both make the technical calls and lead the delivery.

chunks.title: Where has Chris worked, and where does he work now?
chunks.text: Chris's career, most recent first. Now: co-founder and Principal Engineer at Bitcoin Treasury Solutions (March 2025 to present, Melbourne), where he owns the technology end to end. Before that: Juvare, Technical Implementation Analyst (December 2023 to May 2026); Beyond Essential Systems, Software Engineer (September 2021 to December 2023); General Assembly's Software Engineering Immersive (February to August 2021), where he retrained as an engineer; RMIT University, Project Manager for the pandemic response (March to December 2020); and VTAC, Project Manager (November 2014 to March 2020). From 2007 to 2014 he worked in video production and university student administration.

chunks.title: Has he shipped to production?
chunks.text: Yes. business-mono is a live, deployed system that runs every day, not a demo — built and shipped solo, with agents on Railway, the web app on Vercel and a CI-gated test suite. Most of its output is used inside the business rather than sent to customers, and anything that does leave the business goes through human approval.

chunks.title: How does it stay safe?
chunks.text: Through layered controls: approval graduation (human-confirmed to autonomous as trust is earned), always-human gates on emails, published content and CRM writes, and a compliance agent that reviews regulated advice and never auto-approves.

chunks.title: Where is he based / remote?
chunks.text: Chris is based in Melbourne, Australia. He's open to fully remote roles and to hybrid work within Melbourne, but isn't currently looking to relocate.

chunks.title: Is he available?
chunks.text: Chris is open to work now, with a preference for technical product and hands-on AI engineering roles. His Juvare role ended in May 2026. He takes contract, fractional and part-time engagements immediately, and is available full-time from mid-January 2027, alongside co-founding Bitcoin Treasury Solutions with Carolyn Crawford.

chunks.title: VTAC — building and leading the project management office
chunks.text: Alongside managing product at VTAC, Chris ran the project management office, which he grew from one person to six full-time staff between 2018 and 2020. He set the practice up as well as staffing it, using PRINCE2, in which he qualified as a Practitioner in 2016 (the certification has since lapsed): documentation standards, risk and change management, and coordination across developers, testers and UX. It is the clearest example of him leading people, not just delivery.

chunks.title: Chris on listening
chunks.text: A principle Chris has stated consistently across his career: he listens more than he talks, and pays as much attention to what people aren't saying as to what they are. His view is that most people already know the right decision — they need a safe enough room to articulate it. It's why elicitation and human-in-the-loop design keep showing up in the systems he builds.

chunks.title: Chris on owning decisions
chunks.text: The second principle he returns to: don't just make decisions, own them — including the wrong ones. His argument is that visible ownership of mistakes is a net positive for the individual, the team and the organisation, because it lets the team learn and sets a norm of honesty. Easy to say, he notes, and hard to actually do.

chunks.title: Working between engineers and non-technical stakeholders
chunks.text: Chris has spent years as the person in the middle: at VTAC the development team worked in Agile while the university clients expected a waterfall shape, and his job was to find a working balance rather than force either side to convert. He writes user stories, runs discovery, and translates technical constraint into terms a client can make decisions with. Recruiters asking whether he can face a client as well as a codebase have a decade of evidence for it.

chunks.title: Senior stakeholder relationships
chunks.text: Through the VTAC years Chris built and held relationships with senior executives across Victorian universities and education providers — a consortium environment where clients are also owners, and competing interests are the normal condition rather than an exception. He handled client discovery and pricing as well as delivery, so the commercial conversation and the technical one sat with the same person.

chunks.title: Example — growing a project office from one to six
chunks.text: Example (VTAC, 2018–2020). Chris took a project management office that was one person — him — and grew it to six full-time staff over two years, defining how the practice worked as it scaled: documentation, risk and change management grounded in PRINCE2 (he qualified as a Practitioner in 2016; the certification has since lapsed), and how project managers interfaced with an in-house full-stack team building both B2C and B2B applications. Useful answer to 'has he built anything beyond his own output?'

chunks.title: Example — reconciling Agile delivery with waterfall clients
chunks.text: Example (VTAC, FlexiDirect application portal). The internal development team ran Agile; the university and provider clients planned in waterfall, with fixed annual admissions deadlines they could not move. Rather than convert either side, Chris ran the project as a translation layer — iterative internally, milestone-shaped externally — so engineers kept their cadence and clients kept the commitments they needed. Good answer to questions about conflicting stakeholder expectations.

chunks.title: Example — delivering to a hard external deadline alone
chunks.text: Example (Global Vision Media, 2007). On a four-person team producing a community television pilot series, Chris shot, edited and compiled each episode for ingest by Channel 31 at the end of every week — mostly working solo in the edit suite with minimal direction. An early instance of the pattern that shows up again in business-mono: given a deadline and no supervision, the thing ships.

chunks.title: Example — catching what tests miss by reading the output
chunks.text: Example (business-mono, 2025–2026). One of Chris's first workflows produces a daily news email: it takes stories collected and judged in the knowledge base and turns them into a summary with headline links. Live feeds kept surfacing problems that are easy to miss unless you read the output — once, a headline arrived with a raw HTML entity ('&') in it. He only caught it because he reads the email every day; he fixed how headlines are parsed and added the case to the tests. Good answer to 'how do you monitor and tune an agent system once it's live?'

chunks.title: Example — the agent that wasn't needed
chunks.text: Example (business-mono, 2025–2026). Chris designed a coordinator agent as the front door to the whole system, routing every request to specialist agents. In practice it ended up doing far less than planned: most of the platform now runs as structured workflows, because for most jobs a workflow was more reliable and easier to reason about. Good answer to 'tell me about a design decision that didn't work out' or 'when should you not use an agent?'

chunks.title: Example — debugging the dull things first
chunks.text: Example (business-mono, 2025–2026). A recurring lesson from running the platform: plenty of debugging sessions end in the same place — a provider account out of credit. It taught Chris to check the unglamorous causes first before assuming the model or the prompt is at fault.

chunks.title: Is he good with people and stakeholders?
chunks.text: It's the half of the profile most AI engineers don't have. A decade of project and product roles — VTAC, La Trobe, RMIT, Monash, Melbourne, Swinburne — was spent facing clients, executives, academics and students, and the current work carries it forward: client discovery, requirements elicitation, and designing systems that keep a human in the decision. He'd rather run the awkward conversation early than discover the misalignment at delivery.

chunks.title: Has he led a team?
chunks.text: Yes, though it's worth being precise about which kind. He built and led VTAC's project management office, growing it from one person to six between 2018 and 2020, and at Juvare he mentored newer developers locally and remotely, supervised onboarding, and led the rollout of a code-review system. business-mono, by contrast, is a solo build — the evidence there is architectural ownership and the ability to carry a whole system alone, not headcount.

chunks.title: Why did he move from project management into engineering?
chunks.text: Working alongside VTAC's in-house development team is what did it — managing a software product from the non-technical side made him want to build rather than only coordinate. He formalised the move deliberately through General Assembly's immersive in 2021 and went straight into full-stack engineering. He didn't leave delivery behind so much as add the other half to it.

chunks.title: Why bitcoin?
chunks.text: He started Bitcoin Treasury Solutions because he sees bitcoin as a neutral, peaceful money that encourages better human coordination. As bitcoin's users shifted from cypherpunks to investors and companies, he wanted businesses to understand its value proposition properly, as distinct from 'crypto' in general. It's a long-running interest rather than a recent turn — he was following the protocol closely by 2019, running a bitcoin-core full node and experimenting with lightning by 2021, and completed a protocol development seminar series. The business also gave him a real company with real compliance obligations to build production agents against. His personal bitcoin projects sit under the dragon-foobar GitHub account.

chunks.title: Beyond Essential — developer education on Tupaia map configuration (first months)
chunks.text: For his first few months at Beyond Essential Systems, Chris was assigned to developer education — an informal remit rather than a title — for a new visual tool in Tupaia that let non-engineers configure map overlays, working closely with the JSON configuration underneath it. He wrote most of the tool's documentation and onboarded the data analysts who became its primary users, raising issues and improvements as he taught it and then building them himself. He moved into full-stack engineering across the wider codebase from there.

chunks.title: Teaching the tool, then fixing what the teaching exposes
chunks.text: A pattern that recurs in Chris's work: get the users onto the tool, write the documentation, and treat the places they get stuck as the product backlog. At Beyond Essential he onboarded data analysts onto a new map configuration tool in Tupaia and wrote most of its docs, which meant he saw the friction first-hand and could turn it into issues and improvements he then implemented. It is the forward-deployed loop — sit with the users, find what is breaking, ship the fix — rather than collecting feedback and handing it to someone else.

chunks.title: Where to find his code
chunks.text: Chris's code sits across three GitHub accounts, and they do different jobs. avunculargroup is the current one and the one to look at — business-mono and his AI work live there. chris-pollard is the earlier professional account, covering his Beyond Essential Systems work from 2021 to 2023; Tupaia and Tamanu are both public repositories under the beyondessential organisation, so that work is open to inspection — his commits are filterable by author in the Tupaia repository rather than sitting as repos on his own profile. dragon-foobar holds personal projects.

chunks.title: Can I see code he has actually written?
chunks.text: Yes, and without needing anyone's permission. His Beyond Essential commits are public in the Tupaia repository and filterable by author, covering 2021 to 2023 on an open-source platform used for health data in low-resource settings. business-mono, the multi-agent platform, sits under the avunculargroup account. Between them: two years of team engineering in a shared production codebase, and a complete system architected and shipped solo.

chunks.title: Visual craft and design taste
chunks.text: Chris came into software from a visual discipline: a performing arts degree, then two years in video production (2007–2008): partly running his own business, shooting, editing and delivering for paying clients, and partly employed as a camera operator and editor on community television shows. It left him with a trained eye rather than a decorative one, and it shows in the front-end work at Juvare and in how he approaches interface and information design. It is also why design thinking reads as a habit in his work rather than borrowed vocabulary. Running that business — quoting, budgeting, delivering — is the same shape as the fractional engagements he takes now.

chunks.title: Beyond Essential — what he actually built
chunks.text: On Tupaia, Chris built graph and map visualisation features — the charts and geographic overlays that turn aggregated health data into something a decision-maker can read — along with the admin panel UI used to configure them. He also worked on the underlying database structure, built REST APIs and server-side microservices to serve that data, and wrote end-to-end tests across the stack. This is ordinary product engineering in a shared codebase with other engineers, which is the one thing a solo project cannot evidence.

chunks.title: Juvare — government clients and requirements work
chunks.text: At Juvare, Chris's clients were Australian state government agencies, ranging from police through to primary industries. The work was to sit with them, understand their requirements and business processes, and tailor WebEOC into applications that fit how they actually operate — the systems these agencies rely on during incidents. It was forward-deployed work in all but name — the same person ran the discovery conversation and built the result.

chunks.title: Juvare — building inside legacy constraints
chunks.text: Parts of WebEOC run on older technology — jQuery and legacy JavaScript bundles — so building for a client meant working creatively within the limits of the platform rather than reaching for a rewrite. Chris also experimented with introducing web components as a way to modernise incrementally. Relevant to anyone hiring into an established codebase rather than a blank repository.
